Honeycomb MCP Server - Observability Data Query Interface

<role>
You are an observability assistant for Honeycomb users. You investigate production behavior — performance, errors, deployment impact, alert state — by querying real telemetry through these tools. When the user names a dataset, span, or service, treat it as a starting point for discovery, not a license to skip it. The right span name within a dataset is rarely obvious from the dataset name alone, and aggregating the wrong attribute or the wrong span is the most common cause of misleading answers.

Span tools work across all trace-aware datasets in scope without needing to know which dataset to target.

Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

	req := newTrailCreateRequest("title", "body", "feature/x", "main", "open")

	require.Equal(t, api.TrailCreateRequest{
		Title:        "title",
		Body:         "body",
		BranchName:   "feature/x",
		BranchAction: "link",
		Base:         "main",
		Status:       "open",
	}, req)
}

func TestNewTrailCreateRequestCanBeBranchless(t *testing.T) {
	req := newTrailCreateRequest("title", "body", "", "main", "open")

	require.Equal(t, api.TrailCreateRequest{
		Title:  "title",
		Body:   "body",
		Base:   "main",
		Status: "open",
	}, req)

	encoded, err := json.Marshal(req)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NotContains(t, string(encoded), "branch_name")
	require.NotContains(t, string(encoded), "branch_action")
}

func TestPrepareTrailCreateBranchSkipsBranchlessTrail(t *testing.T) {
	state, err := prepareTrailCreateBranch(io.Discard, io.Discard, nil, "", "main", true)

	require.False(t, state.NeedsCreation)
	require.False(t, state.LocalCreated)
	require.False(t, state.RemotePushed)
}

- **Branchless trails:** Created by omitting `--branch` or passing `--no-branch`; these have no branch binding
- **Branch relationship:** Trails are keyed by:

  - **Trail ID** (UUID, for review/finding operations)
  - **Branch name** (for lookups via `findTrailByBranch`, trail_cmd.go:1499)

The "shadow" aspect: Trails shadow a PR-like workflow by binding metadata (title, body, status, labels, reviewers) to a branch, but operate as an independent entity on the server (with their own ID, separate from GitHub PR numbers).

content.text:
## Review: PR #1492 — "Support branchless trail creation"

I reviewed the actual delta (the `5921e409c` commit — the 231/113 in the PR matches it exactly; everything else in `main..HEAD` is already on main via merges) and mapped the whole `trail` command surface. Build ✅, `trail` tests ✅, lint clean on the changed files ✅.

### What the change does
1. `TrailCreateRequest.BranchName` becomes `omitempty`; `newTrailCreateRequest` omits **both** `branch_name` and `branch_action` when branch is empty → server creates a branchless trail.
2. New `--no-branch` flag on `trail create`.
3. Splits the monolithic `runTrailCreate` into focused, testable helpers (`resolveTrailCreateBase`, `resolveTrailCreateFields`, `validateTrailCreateFields`, `prepareTrailCreateBranch`, `ensureTrailCreateBranchExists`, `postTrailCreate`, `printTrailCreateResult`, `maybeCheckoutTrailCreateBranch`).
4. Flag-combo guards: `--no-branch` rejects `--branch` and `--checkout`.
5. Interactive flow skips the branch step (asks only Title/Body/Status) when branchless.

### Assessment: solid, ship-worthy refactor
The extraction genuinely improves readability and testability, and the branchless path is threaded cleanly. The interactive-detection logic (`!changed("title") && !changed("branch")`) still behaves correctly across all four `--no-branch` permutations I traced. A nice incidental improvement: the API client/auth is now resolved **before** pushing the branch, so an auth failure no longer pushes a branch you then have to clean up.

### Findings

**1. Test coverage gap (medium).** Only `newTrailCreateRequest` and the trivial early-return in `prepareTrailCreateBranch` are tested. The user-facing guardrails and flows are untested:
- `validateTrailCreateFlagCombos` (the `--no-branch`+`--branch`/`--checkout` rejections) — no test.
- The interactive branchless flow (`runTrailCreateInteractive` with `noBranch=true`).
- A full branchless `runTrailCreate` happy path. `trail_cmd_test.go` already has an `httptest` harness, so a "create branchless trail, assert request omits branch fields and output says `Created trail "X" (ID: …)`" test would be cheap and high-value.

**2. Cross-repo server contract (verify before merge).** This depends on the entire backend accepting a POST with neither `branch_name` nor `branch_action`. This PR is CLI-only. Confirm the server side has landed (or is gated) — otherwise `entire trail create --no-branch` fails against prod. (The PR is itself linked to trail 634, so presumably the backend work is tracked alongside.)

**3. Vestigial logic in `maybeCheckoutTrailCreateBranch` (low/cosmetic).** The `checkout = true` reassignment inside the form block is redundant now that `shouldCheckout` holds the answer — the function could check `if !shouldCheckout { return nil }` and drop the `checkout` var entirely. Carried over from the original; not worth blocking on.

### The `trail` surface, for context
`trail` is a hidden top-level command requiring auth; all endpoints under `/api/v1/trails/{forge}/{owner}/{repo}`:
- **Core:** `show`, `list`, `create`, `update`, `checkout`, `delete`
- **`trail finding`** (review findings): `list`, `add`, `show`, `update`, `apply`, `resolve`, `dismiss`, `reopen` → `…/reviews/...` endpoints
- **`trail watch`**: SSE stream of finding events

The branch model: trails normally bind to a remote branch via `BranchAction: "link"` (CLI pushes the branch first, then creates the trail). This PR adds the third mode — no branch at all — alongside the existing "link existing" and "create new" branch behaviors. The change is consistent with that existing design.

Net: clean, well-factored, correct. I'd ask for the branchless end-to-end + flag-combo tests and confirmation the backend accepts branchless creates before merging.

The displayed cache-read figure in the recommendation message (`Cache/context replay is X% of token volume`) will also under-report. Consider computing the percentage against a top-level-only total (input+cacheCreation+cacheRead+output) or otherwise aligning numerator and denominator scope.

- **Inconsistent rounding between two percent helpers** — `session_tokens.go`: context pressure uses `roundedPercent` (round-half-up, clamped 0–100), while cache-read uses `tokenPercent` (float, truncated to one decimal in `formatPercent`). In practice the data is JSON-deserialized (acyclic), so this cannot occur from real inputs; flagging only for completeness, not as something to fix.

// formatTokenCount formats a token count for display.
// 0 → "0", 500 → "500", 1200 → "1.2k", 14300 → "14.3k"
func formatTokenCount(n int) string {
	if n < 1000 {
		return strconv.Itoa(n)
	}
	f := float64(n) / 1000.0
	s := fmt.Sprintf("%.1f", f)
	// Remove trailing ".0" for clean display (e.g., 1000 → "1k" not "1.0k")
	s = strings.TrimSuffix(s, ".0")
	return s + "k"
}

// totalTokens recursively sums all token fields including subagent tokens.
func totalTokens(tu *agent.TokenUsage) int {

	total = saturatingIntAdd(total, tu.CacheReadTokens)
	total = saturatingIntAdd(total, tu.OutputTokens)
	total = saturatingIntAdd(total, totalTokens(tu.SubagentTokens))

}

func saturatingIntAdd(a, b int) int {
	maxValue := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	minValue := -maxValue - 1
	if b > 0 && a > maxValue-b {
		return maxValue
	}
	if b < 0 && a < minValue-b {
		return minValue
	}
	return a + b
}

func saturatingIntSub(a, b int) int {
	if b < 0 {
		if b == minInt() {
			if a >= 0 {
				return maxInt()
			}
			return a - b
		}
		if a > maxInt()-(-b) {
			return maxInt()
		}
	}
	if b > 0 && a < minInt()+b {
		return minInt()
	}
	return a - b
}

func maxInt() int { return int(^uint(0) >> 1) }
func minInt() int { return -maxInt() - 1 }

func FindMostRecentSession(ctx context.Context) string {

**Concern A — `roundedPercent` overflow guard correctness.** Let me trace the `bits` math:
```go
hi, lo := bits.Mul64(uint64(value), 100)        // 128-bit product value*100
lo, carry := bits.Add64(lo, uint64(total)/2, 0) // add total/2 for rounding
hi += carry
divisor := uint64(total)
if hi >= divisor { return maxPercent }           // guard: Div64 panics if hi>=divisor
quotient, _ := bits.Div64(hi, lo, divisor)
```
`value` and `total` come from context tokens / window size, both `int`, cast to `uint64`. They're non-negative (guarded by `buildSessionTokensContext` requiring `tokens>0, windowSize>0`). The guard prevents the panic. This is heavily over-engineered for values that realistically fit in int64*100 without 128-bit math, but it's correct. Not a finding.

**Concern B — the `--compare` percent uses `change/baseline`, and Total can legitimately be 0** when baseline checkpoint has API-call-only usage. `buildCheckpointMetricDelta` guards `if baseline != 0`. But note: it builds deltas for Total, CacheRead, AND APICalls. For CacheRead, baseline CacheRead could be 0 while Total nonzero → ChangePercent nil for that metric → printed without percent. Handled. Good.

Now, the genuinely notable issue: **the comparison only requires `target.Tokens != nil && baseline.Tokens != nil`**, but `buildSessionTokensUsage` returns a non-nil struct with `Total==0` for API-call-only usage. So `buildCheckpointMetricDelta(0, 0)` for Total → change 0, direction unchanged, status `observed_no_change`. That's reasonable, not a bug.

Let me look for the actual medium+ issues. The strongest candidate is the spec/description mismatch and the `resolveExplainCheckpointID` lookup leak. Let me verify the leak path in `loadCheckpointTokensReport`.

In `loadCheckpointTokensReport`:
```go
cpID, lookup, err := resolveExplainCheckpointID(...)
if err != nil {
    return checkpointTokensReport{}, lookup, err   // returns lookup
}
```
And the caller `runCheckpointTokens`:
```go
report, lookup, err := loadCheckpointTokensReport(...)
if lookup != nil {
    defer lookup.Close()
}
if err != nil {
    return tokenCommandError(err)
}
```
The caller closes `lookup` even on error. Good — no leak in the primary path. And the baseline path also defers `baselineLookup.Close()`. So the lookup leak the subagent worried about is actually **handled correctly** here. Good.

Now let me reconsider the **"branch average" / "recommend cheaper model"** description. The code implements neither. This is the most important reviewer note: the PR description (and command help could imply more) oversells. But the help text itself (`--compare`, recommendations) accurately describes pairwise comparison and the actual rule-based recommendations. So this is a description-vs-implementation gap for the reviewer to flag, not a code defect.

Let me look at one more real concern: in `buildCheckpointTokensReport`, when `len(metas) > 1`, it sums `turnCount` across metas but only builds `report.Context` for the single-session case. For multi-session, context pressure is silently dropped. That's a deliberate scoping choice (per-session context windows don't sum meaningfully), and is documented by the aggregate-scope test. Reasonable, not a bug.

Let me check the `report.Agent` single-value vs the text output. In `writeCheckpointTokensText`, the `switch` has a `case report.Agent != ""` branch — but `report.Agent` is only set when `len(metas)==1`. For multi-session, `SessionCount>1` branch handles it. For single session with `SessionID==""`... unlikely. Fine.

I have enough to write the review. Let me also double check the `saturatingIntSub` min-int path is tested (it is: `TestSaturatingIntSubHandlesMinIntSubtrahend`) and correct. For `a>=0, b==minInt`: returns maxInt. `a - minInt = a + (maxInt+1)`, for a>=0 that overflows, so returning maxInt (saturate) is correct. For `a<0, b==minInt`: `a-b = a-minInt = a+maxInt+1`, a in [minInt,-1] → result in [0,maxInt], no overflow, correct.

I have a complete picture. Here is my review.

---

## SUMMARY

This change adds two read-only reporting commands: `entire session tokens [session-id]` (with `--current`, `--json`, and `--agent-brief` modes) and `entire checkpoint tokens <id>` (with `--compare <id>`). Both build a structured report from already-captured token/context/skill metadata and emit rule-based optimization recommendations (cache-replay hotspots, API-call amplification, subagent-heavy usage, high context pressure, long sessions). The implementation is careful and well-tested: token sums are overflow-hardened end-to-end (`saturatingIntAdd`/`saturatingIntSub`, a 128-bit `roundedPercent`), division-by-zero is guarded in every percentage path, context cancellation is propagated, and the not-found/missing-metadata cases degrade gracefully with explicit limitations. Conventions are respected — output goes through `cmd.OutOrStdout()`/`ErrOrStderr()`, the `SilentError` pattern is used for already-printed messages, only operational metadata is emitted (no prompts/file contents), and the lookup handle from `resolveExplainCheckpointID` is closed on every path including errors. Test parallelism follows the repo rule (pure-function tests use `t.Parallel()`; `t.Chdir`-based command tests correctly omit it). Overall this is high quality and close to mergeable; my findings are mostly a spec-vs-implementation mismatch and a few medium polish items, with no high-severity correctness bug found.

## FINDINGS (medium+)

**[MEDIUM] PR description vs. implementation mismatch — no "branch average" comparison and no "switch model" recommendation.** *(checkpoint_tokens.go, whole comparison path; session_tokens.go `recommendationRules` ~L230-300)*
The PR brief states `checkpoint tokens` "compares a checkpoint's token usage against the branch average" and "recommends optimizations like switching models or enabling prompt caching." The code does neither: `--compare` is a strictly pairwise comparison against one user-supplied baseline checkpoint (`buildCheckpointTokensComparison`), there is no branch-average aggregation anywhere, and `recommendationRules` never emits a model-switch or prompt-caching recommendation (its rules cover cache-replay, API-call count, subagents, context pressure, and long sessions). The code itself is internally consistent and its `--help` text is accurate, so this is a description/scope gap rather than a code defect — but it should be reconciled before merge so reviewers and users aren't expecting branch-average or cost/model advice the command doesn't provide.

**[MEDIUM] `--compare` qualification can mislead because per-session cache state isn't normalized.** *(checkpoint_tokens.go, `checkpointComparisonQualification` / `buildCheckpointMetricDelta` ~L380-420)*
The comparison reports `observed_reduction` / `observed_increase` purely from the signed delta of summed `Total` tokens between two checkpoints. Because `Total` includes `CacheReadTokens` (large-context replays), a checkpoint that simply had more cache reads will read as an "increase" and a cache-warmed follow-up as a "reduction," independent of actual work done. The qualification strings do hedge ("does not prove quality was preserved"), which is good, but the directional verdict itself is driven by a metric dominated by cache replay. Consider qualifying the verdict on the non-cache delta (input+output) or surfacing the cache-read delta as the headline caveat, so "reduction"/"increase" isn't dominated by replay volume.

**[MEDIUM] `recommendationRules` and the agent-brief use fixed magic thresholds with no provenance.** *(session_tokens.go `recommendationRules` ~L235-300)*
The thresholds — cache-read `>= 80%` (high), API calls `>= 20` (medium), subagent share `>= 10%`, context `>= 80%`, turn count `>= 10` / checkpoint count `>= 5` — are hardcoded inline with no named constants or comment explaining their basis. These directly drive user- and agent-facing advice (the agent-brief literally tells an agent to "batch the next diagnostic step" / "compact or restart"). They are defensible defaults, but as written they're unexplained and untunable. Extract them into named constants with a one-line rationale so the behavior is reviewable and adjustable without hunting through the rule body.

## Low-severity nits

- **Inconsistent int-limit helpers** (`checkpoint_tokens.go`): `saturatingIntAdd` computes `maxValue`/`minValue` inline while `saturatingIntSub` uses the `maxInt()`/`minInt()` helpers. Use the helpers in both for consistency.
- **`roundedPercent` is over-engineered** (`session_tokens.go`): it uses `bits.Mul64`/`bits.Div64` 128-bit math for values (context tokens, window size) that comfortably fit in `int64*100`. Correct, but a plain `(value*100 + total/2)/total` on `int64` would be far easier to read; the 128-bit version is justified only if these can realistically approach 1e16.
- **`buildCheckpointTokensReport` drops context pressure for multi-session checkpoints** (`checkpoint_tokens.go` ~L200-230): context info and the `context_pressure` contributor are only populated when `len(metas)==1`. This is a defensible choice (per-session context windows don't sum), and it is covered by `...UsesAggregateScope`, but it's silent — a one-line limitation note for the multi-session case would make the omission explicit to users.
- **`addCheckpointTokenUsage` enumerates fields manually** (`checkpoint_tokens.go`): it copies the five scalar fields plus `SubagentTokens` by hand. If `agent.TokenUsage` gains a field later, aggregation will silently drop it. A brief comment ("update when TokenUsage gains fields") or a small unit test asserting field coverage would guard against drift.

No data races (all paths are single-goroutine, request-scoped), no nil-deref (every `*TokenUsage`/`*SessionMetrics`/`state` is nil-checked, and `LoadSessionState`/`ReadCommitted` nil-returns are handled), and no privacy violations (only IDs, counts, model names, and skill labels are emitted) were found.

content.text:
All findings posted. Here's the consolidated review of the three trails.

---

## Context: these are three competing iterations of the same feature

All three are by the same author (`peyton-alt`), all branch off `main`, all add token-usage diagnostics, and they share the same wiring files and a growing common core (`checkpoint_tokens.go`, `session_tokens.go`, the overflow-safe `totalTokens` in `status_style.go`). They look like escalating drafts: `tokens` (smallest) → `tokens-agent-brief` → `tokens-profile` (largest). Worth deciding which one to land rather than reviewing them as independent features.

Common positives across all three: output goes through `cmd.Out/ErrOrStderr()`, the `SilentError` pattern is used correctly, token sums are overflow-hardened (`saturatingIntAdd/Sub`, 128-bit percent math), division-by-zero is guarded everywhere, missing/unreadable metadata degrades gracefully, and **no prompt/file content is printed or exported** — only operational metadata. Test coverage is genuinely behavioral and follows the repo's `t.Chdir`-no-`t.Parallel()` discipline. None of the three has a high-severity bug.

---

### Trail 542 — `tokens` (Token usage diagnostics)
The base variant: `entire session tokens` + `entire checkpoint tokens <id>`. Cleanest and smallest; high quality.
**Posted (1 medium):**
- Cache-replay percentage mixes a top-level numerator (`CacheRead`) with a subagent-inclusive denominator (`Total`), so the percentage is systematically understated when subagents are present and the context-replay recommendation can fail to fire.

*Low nits (not posted):* two percent helpers round differently; `Agent`/`Agents` both populated for single-session; two tests skip `t.Parallel()` unnecessarily.

### Trail 547 — `tokens-agent-brief` (Token guidance and checkpoint comparison)
Adds `--agent-brief` mode and `checkpoint tokens --compare <id>`. The lookup-handle and division paths are all handled correctly.
**Posted (3 medium):**
- **Description vs. implementation gap** — the trail promises "compare against branch average" and "recommend switching models"; the code does neither (only pairwise `--compare`, and no model/caching recommendation rule exists).
- `--compare`'s reduction/increase verdict is driven by `Total`, which is dominated by cache replays — a cache-warmed follow-up reads as a "reduction" regardless of actual work.
- Recommendation thresholds (80% cache, 20 API calls, etc.) are hardcoded magic numbers with no constants/rationale, yet they drive agent-facing advice.

### Trail 559 — `tokens-profile` (Token profile history diagnostics)
Largest: adds the labs-gated `entire tokens profile` (cross-checkpoint aggregation + JSON export). Labs wiring is consistent (`Hidden`, registered, advertised, test-verified). Note: no CSV export / date-range filtering despite the description implying them.
**Posted (2 medium):**
- `--current` flag is a **no-op** — `FindMostRecentSession` already scopes to the current worktree, so `session tokens` and `session tokens --current` are identical; the help text promises behavior that doesn't exist.
- `tokens profile` and `checkpoint tokens` use **different precedence rules** for a checkpoint with partially-unreadable session metadata (root summary vs. per-session aggregate), so they can report different totals for the same checkpoint. Should share one rule.

---

Total: **6 medium findings** posted (1 → 542, 3 → 547, 2 → 559). No high-severity issues, no privacy problems. The most actionable items are the 547 description/scope mismatch and the 559 `--current` no-op, since both are user-visible promises the code doesn't keep. One cross-cutting note worth raising with the author: the cache-read-vs-total denominator/verdict issue shows up in more than one branch, so whichever variant lands should fix it once in the shared code.

ULID is case-sensitive canonical uppercase, but the resolver accepts lowercase too. The concern flagged in the code comment: a 26-char name matching the alphabet would be misread. Also note — could a legitimate org/project *name* be a valid ULID shape? Names like generated identifiers. Low risk, acknowledged in comments. 

One more: case sensitivity in name matching. `pickOrg`/`pickProject` use exact `==` (case-sensitive). If the server's `ListProjects --name` filter is case-insensitive but `pickProject` is case-sensitive, a name differing only in case would be filtered-in by the server then dropped by `pickProject` → "no project named". This is the kind of subtle mismatch worth flagging. Let me check whether the server name filter is case-sensitive — I can't see server code, but the spec just says "exact-match". ## SUMMARY

This PR is **518/22 lines, entirely hand-written** — the ogen-generated `coreapi` methods it consumes (`ResolveHandle`, `ListOrgProjects`, `RevokeProjectAccessByProvider`) already exist on `main`, so this delta is pure CLI wiring plus a new `resolveref.go` resolver layer. The work is clean, well-commented, and idiomatic: it correctly threads name→ULID resolution inside the `runCore*` closures (so `SilenceUsage` and `renderCoreError` apply), uses the established `cmd.Printf` output convention, and does **not** re-resolve the control-plane core target anywhere (no `auth.ResolveControlPlaneTarget()` misuse — the only new print uses literal args). Name resolution handles the three cases that matter — ULID passthrough with no network call, no-match with an actionable error, and ambiguity that lists candidate ULIDs — and `projectGranteeMode` cleanly enforces the mutually-exclusive grantee addressing modes. The pure helpers (`looksLikeULID`, `parseQualifiedHandle`, `pickOrg`, `pickProject`, `filterProjectsByName`, `projectGranteeMode`) have solid table-driven tests with correct `t.Parallel()` usage. **Overall judgment: APPROVE** — the findings below are medium-and-below; none block merge.

---

## MEDIUM+ FINDINGS

**[MEDIUM] Case-sensitivity mismatch between server name filter and client-side `pickProject` — `cmd/entire/cli/resolveref.go` ~line 78 (`resolveProjectRef`) / ~line 116 (`pickProject`)**
`resolveProjectRef` delegates name filtering to the server via `ListProjects{Name: ...}` (documented "exact-match"), then `pickProject` re-filters with a case-sensitive Go `p.Name == name`. If the server's exact-match is case-insensitive (common for names), a query like `--project Widgets` against a project named `widgets` would be returned by the server but dropped by `pickProject`, producing a misleading "no project named" error instead of resolving. Worth confirming the server filter's case behavior; if it is case-insensitive, either normalize before comparing or drop the redundant client-side re-check and trust the server result. The same pattern applies to `pickOrg`, which filters a full `ListOrgs` client-side with `==`.

**[MEDIUM] `resolveAccountRef` assumes a non-empty `AccountId` from `ResolveHandle` — `cmd/entire/cli/resolveref.go` ~line 53**
`resolveAccountRef` returns `id.AccountId` directly after `ResolveHandle`. `ResolvedIdentity.AccountId` is a plain (non-optional) string, so if the server ever resolves a handle to an identity with no backing account (or returns 200 with an empty `accountId`), this silently forwards `""` as the owner ULID into `CreateProjectInputBody.OwnerId`, deferring failure to an opaque server-side create error. A guard — `if id.AccountId == "" { return "", fmt.Errorf("handle %q resolved to no account", ref) }` — would turn a confusing downstream error into a clear local one. Low likelihood but cheap insurance at an external boundary.

**[LOW-MEDIUM] Resolver functions (the network-branching logic) are untested despite an available harness — `cmd/entire/cli/resolveref.go` / `resolveref_test.go`**
The pure helpers are well covered, but `resolveOrgRef`/`resolveProjectRef`/`resolveAccountRef` — which contain the actual ULID-vs-name branch and the "ULID makes no network call" guarantee called out as load-bearing in the file's doc comment — have no tests. `repo_mirror_test.go` already establishes the `coreapi.NewWithBearer(httptest.NewServer(...).URL, "tok")` pattern, so a test asserting that a ULID ref issues zero HTTP requests while a name ref issues exactly one list call would be modest effort and would lock in the key invariant. Not a blocker given the helper coverage, but it leaves the most regression-prone seam unguarded.

---

## LOW NITS

- **`cmd/entire/cli/resolveref.go` ~line 137 (`pickProject` ambiguity message)**: the error tells the user to "run `entire project list --org <org>`" to find the ULID, but the user is mid-`repo create`/`grant project` and may not know which org to pass — the comment above the function even acknowledges these callers have no `--org`. Minor; the listed candidate ULIDs already let the user proceed, so the suggestion is just slightly aspirational.
- **`projectGranteeMode` returns `0` (== `granteeModeProvider`) on every error path** (`cmd/entire/cli/grant.go`). Harmless because every caller checks `err != nil` first, but returning the zero value of a *valid* mode on error is a small latent foot-gun; an explicit invalid sentinel would read more defensively. Not worth changing on its own.
- The `--name` + `--org` combination in `project list` silently applies `--name` client-side (documented in the code comment), which is fine, but there's no user-facing note that `--name` semantics differ subtly between the two paths (server exact-match vs. client `filterProjectsByName` exact-match). They happen to agree on exact-match, so no behavioral divergence today.

No issues found with control-plane core resolution (correctly avoided `ResolveControlPlaneTarget` for display), settings/logging conventions, or the `SilentError` path.

Confirmed both findings directly against the code. Here's the review of trail 613.

---

## Trail 613 — Adopt active sessions across repos and worktrees (`feat/session-adopt`) · +1534 / −5

**Verdict: approve-with-reservations.** Adds `entire session adopt [session-id] --from <worktree>`, which reads the source `.git/entire-sessions` store and writes target-local session state (HEAD, branch, worktree path, worktree ID) so the target repo's post-commit hook can link the session and emit an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer. The high-risk plumbing is sound: store resolution goes through `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` + `EvalSymlinks` (`stateStoreForWorktree`, :194) rather than `os.Getwd()`, the same-vs-external store split is decided correctly by comparing common-dirs (:82), the worktree ID is captured identically to a live session (`GetWorktreeID(WorktreeRoot)`), the deep-clone of source state is thorough (token usage, skill events, prompt attributions, time pointers), and the ended/condensed rejection plus transcript-ownership validation are in place. The ~1000-line test file exercises real behavior (state written to the target common-dir, source untouched, rejection paths), and the three edits to `state.go`/`manual_commit.go`/`open.go` are backward-compatible. Both reservations below are hardening of an already-correct path, not correctness breakers.

### Medium findings

**1. [MEDIUM] External-store adopt acts on a stale, unlocked source snapshot — `session_adopt.go:87` + `adoptFromExternalSessionStore` :116**
`runAdopt` loads `sourceState` once via `selectAdoptSourceSession` (:87), an unlocked `store.Load`. The same-store path then re-reads and re-validates the source *inside* a lock via `strategy.MutateSessionState` (:146 — it re-checks `isAdoptableSourceSession`, worktree ownership, and the transcript on the freshly-loaded `current`). The external path does neither: it passes the snapshot captured at :87 straight into `buildAdoptedSessionState` and writes it to the target. If the source session is ended/condensed or advances between that initial read and the write, the external adopt proceeds on stale data and can anchor a session that is no longer adoptable. Mirror the same-store path: re-load and re-validate the source under its lock before building the adopted state.

**2. [MEDIUM] External target write is a lock-free read-modify-write (TOCTOU) — `session_adopt.go:121-130`**
`adoptFromExternalSessionStore` does `targetStore.Load` (existence/`--force` check, :121-127) then `targetStore.Save` (:128) with no lock held on the target store. The same-store path routes its write through `strategy.MutateSessionState`, which serializes the read-modify-write; the external write path has no equivalent. A concurrent adopt or a target-repo hook writing the same session state can interleave between the Load and the Save, dropping one of the writes or racing the `--force` existence check. Wrap the external target Load+Save in the same locked mutation primitive the same-store path uses.

### Low nits
- The "one recent active source session" auto-pick lives in `selectAdoptSourceSession` (:229) and is reasonable, but worth confirming the ambiguity message is actionable when multiple recent active sessions exist.
- `stateStoreForWorktree` parses exactly two lines from `rev-parse` (:212-215); fine, but brittle if git output format ever changes — the explicit length check mitigates it.

---

Net: the cross-repo/worktree resolution and field capture are correct and well-tested; the two reservations are a **consistency gap between the same-store and external-store paths** — the same-store path locks and re-validates, the external path doesn't. Worth closing before merge since cross-repo adopt is exactly when concurrent hooks are likely.

Description:
Problem: The entire trail command let you create, check out, and update trails, but there was no quick way to jump back into the agent session tied to a trail. To pick up work you had to manually find the right branch, locate the checkpoint, restore its session logs, and then remember and run the correct agent-specific resume command. This was especially painful when the local session state was gone and the only record lived in committed checkpoints.
Solution: Adds a new entire trail resume subcommand that takes you from a trail straight back into its agent session.
You can name the trail by number, id, or branch, or let it default to the current branch's trail.
It prints a context overview first: trail details, the checkpoint sessions on the branch (id, agent, last active, prompt), open review findings, and ready-to-copy commands.
It restores session logs from the branch's latest checkpoint (or a specific one via --checkpoint/--session), reading directly from committed checkpoint data so it works even when local session state is missing.

## Review: PR #1511 / trail 650 — `trail: add resume command` (+2276/−90 → main, CI green)

**Verdict: approve (one test-coverage reservation).** This is a well-built, carefully-factored feature. I verified all four high-risk areas and they're sound:

- **`resume.go` refactor — no regression.** Each `resume*` function was split into a `restore*` that returns `[]RestoredSession` plus a thin wrapper that calls the unchanged `displayRestoredSessions`. The existing `entire resume`/`session resume` output is preserved (the resume command is still printed via the wrapper; the early-return branches that used to print it now return a populated `RestoredSession` and the wrapper prints once). `findBranchCheckpoints` was parameterized to resolve an arbitrary branch (local or `origin/<branch>`) without altering the HEAD path. `RestoredSession` gains two additive fields.

The actual log-restore mechanics are untouched — no working-tree write, no `git reset`, no `.entire/` exposure.
- **Exec safety.** `NewForegroundCommand` does `LookPath` + `exec.CommandContext(ctx, bin, args...)` — argv, **no shell** — so session IDs can't inject. Stdio is wired to the real terminal (correct for an interactive foreground agent).
- **Launch gating.** Non-interactive runs (`!CanPromptInteractively()`) **never launch** — they print commands. `launchTrailRestoredSession` degrades gracefully when an agent has no `ResumeLauncher` or the launch errors (falls back to printing). Per-agent flags all match their `FormatResumeCommand` (verified claude `-r`, gemini `--resume`, etc.), and the `ResumeLauncher` interface is optional via a clean type-assertion.

### Medium finding

content.text:
Based on the gating logic in `trail_resume_cmd.go` (the resume-decision block) and `launchTrailRestoredSession` → `agent.NewResumeForegroundCommand`, here's exactly when `entire trail resume` **directly launches** the agent versus just printing the resume command.

## It directly launches only when ALL of these hold

1. **`--no-resume` was not passed.** With `--no-resume` it only prints the context overview and stops.
2. **You're in an interactive terminal** — `interactive.CanPromptInteractively()` is true. That means a real TTY: not CI, not piped/redirected, not under test, not an agent-sentinel environment. In any non-interactive case it always **prints** the command(s) instead of launching.
3. **At least one session was restored** from the checkpoint.
4. **A single session is unambiguously chosen.** Specifically one of:
   - you selected one explicitly via `--session`/`--checkpoint`, or
   - the branch's checkpoint has exactly one session, or
   - there were several and you **picked one in the interactive picker**.
5. **The session's agent is in the launchable set** — `ResumeCommandSpecFor` returns ok for: **claude, codex, copilot, droid, gemini, opencode, pi**. Cursor (and any unknown agent) are print-only → it prints the command.
6. **A usable session ID exists for that agent.** For claude / codex / copilot / droid / gemini, an **empty** session ID → print-only (it won't spawn `claude -r ""`). opencode and pi are the exception: they launch even with an empty ID (bare `opencode` / `pi --continue`).
7. **The agent binary is found on `PATH`.** `NewForegroundCommand` does a `LookPath`; if the binary isn't installed, it prints "Could not launch … / To continue this session: …" and falls back to the command string.

When it does launch, it runs the agent **in the foreground** wired to your terminal (`stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr`), after printing `Launching: <cmd>`.

## So it just PRINTS the command (never launches) when

- `--no-resume` is set, **or**
- the run is non-interactive (CI, piped output, no TTY), **or**
- the agent is cursor / not launchable, **or**
- the session ID is empty for one of the five strict agents, **or**
- the agent binary isn't on `PATH`.

## Quick mental model

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Interactive TTY, 1 session, launchable agent, binary present | **Launches** |
| Interactive TTY, multiple sessions | Shows picker → **launches** your pick |
| Interactive, `--session`/`--checkpoint` chosen | **Launches** that one |
| Non-interactive / piped / CI | **Prints** command(s) |
| `--no-resume` | Context only, **no** restore/launch |
| Cursor agent, or binary missing, or empty ID (claude/codex/copilot/droid/gemini) | **Prints** command |

One nuance worth noting: the interactive single-session path launches **without a confirmation prompt** — it restores and immediately spawns the agent. If you'd prefer a "Launch now? [y/N]" gate before it takes over the terminal, that'd be a reasonable enhancement (and isn't currently there). Want me to flag that on the trail?

Re-reviewed PR #1499 at the current HEAD. The picture is now crisp — and there's one thing you'll want to know about.

## PR #1499 re-review (now targets **main** directly, +1122/−116)

The `feat/control-plane-friendly-names` base merged to main, so this is no longer stacked. Several commits landed since last time (`confirm destructive ... delete`, `idempotent deletes + command-level wiring tests`, `show resolved ULID in delete success messages`).

### Typed deletes (org / project / repo) — **FULLY ADDRESSED** ✅
All three of the original concerns are now closed for the typed verbs:
- **Confirmation + `--force`:** `org.go:102`, `project.go:181`, `repo.go:186` all route through `runControlPlaneDelete` and register `addForceFlag`.
- **Idempotency:** `TestControlPlaneDelete_Wiring` (`corecmd_delete_test.go:62`) asserts a 404 → `"not found; nothing to delete"`.
- **Wiring tests:** that same test drives all three through cobra+httptest — `--force` issues `DELETE`, and a non-interactive run without `--force` **refuses**.

### Grant remove/revoke (org / project / repo) — **STILL UNADDRESSED** ❌
The grant-revoke surface I flagged last round was **not** touched:
- **No confirmation / no `--force`.** `newGrantRepoRemoveCmd` (`grant.go:451`), `newGrantOrgRemoveCmd` (`:175`), `newGrantProjectRemoveCmd` (`:282`) still call `RevokeRepoAccess(ByProvider)` / `RemoveOrgMember` / `RevokeProjectAccess(ByProvider)` immediately after resolving the ref. None register `addForceFlag` or call `runControlPlaneDelete`.
- **Not idempotent.** Each is `if err := c.Revoke…(); err != nil { return err }` — raw error, no `isCoreNotFound` guard, so a second revoke still surfaces a 404.
- **No route-mapping test.** `grant_test.go` is still only `TestValidateGrantRole` / `TestParseGranteeMode` / `TestParseOrgRole`; nothing exercises the `--provider` → by-provider vs typed-id route selection.

### ⚠️ Discrepancy worth your attention
On trail #642, the grant route-mapping finding (`019ef8f0-f3f`, `grant_test.go`) is marked **resolved** — but the code shows **no such test exists**. That resolution looks premature/incorrect. The other two grant findings (the `grant.go` confirmation + idempotency ones) were cleared as *stale* on the rebase and no longer appear, even though both are still valid in the current code.

### My read
The team did a clean job on the **delete** verbs (good shared helper + real wiring tests), but the **grant-revoke** verbs were left in exactly the state I flagged — and one of those findings got marked resolved without a corresponding fix. Worth noting that revoking a grant is reversible (you can re-grant), so the *confirmation* gap is lower-stakes than the irreversible org/project delete; the idempotency and missing-test points stand on their own regardless.

I haven't changed anything. Want me to **reopen** the incorrectly-resolved test finding (and re-post the two stale-pruned grant findings) on trail #642, or leave them as-is?

content.text:
Re-reviewed trail 652 at the current HEAD — **both my findings are addressed.** The code genuinely changed (not just the main merges); my findings had been cleared as stale, and I verified the fixes directly.

## Trail 652 re-review (`dip/trail-context-cache-refresh`)

### F1 — Non-atomic load-modify-save race on clone-preferences → **ADDRESSED** ✅
The fix is exactly right. `saveTrailsEnabledForScope` now goes through a new `settings.ModifyClonePreferences(ctx, fn)` → `modifyClonePreferencesFile`, which:
```go
release, err := flock.Acquire(filePath + ".lock")   // acquire file lock
defer release()
prefs, err := loadClonePreferencesFromFile(filePath) // load
fn(prefs)                                            // mutate
return saveClonePreferencesToFile(prefs, filePath)   // save
```
The entire read-modify-write now runs **inside a cross-process file lock**, so concurrent hooks (multiple worktrees/sessions, the interactive picker) can no longer interleave and clobber each other's writes. This closes the lost-write race I flagged.

### F2 — ~3s synchronous network on cold SessionStart → **ADDRESSED (mitigated)** ✅
They split the timeout into a dedicated, shorter constant for the startup path:
```go
trailEnablementSessionStartRefreshTimeout = time.Second       // 1s — SessionStart
trailEnablementRefreshTimeout             = 3 * time.Second   // 3s — other paths
```
`lifecycle.go` now bounds the SessionStart refresh to **1s** (down from 3s), via `context.WithTimeout(ctx, trailEnablementSessionStartRefreshTimeout)`. My finding asked to "confirm 3s is acceptable or shorten/async it" — they shortened the worst-case startup delay to 1s while keeping 3s for non-startup refreshes. A deliberate, reasonable response.

### Residual (minor, was the secondary half of F2)
The SessionStart refresh is **still synchronous** (not backgrounded) — it's just bounded to 1s now. So a cold/stale cache still adds up to ~1s to agent session startup. That's a much smaller, defensible cost, and consistent with the "best-effort, errors logged and ignored" design (the refresh error path just `logging.Debug`s and continues). If even 1s of startup latency matters, backgrounding it would eliminate it entirely — but I'd consider this resolved as-is.

---

Both findings resolved with solid fixes (the file lock in particular is the correct, complete answer to the race). The trail has no open findings, and I haven't posted or changed anything. Nothing new rose to a medium worth flagging.

content.text:
Reviewed trail 661 — clean, low-risk change. **Verdict: approve, no medium+ findings.**

## Trail 661 — Collect installed git version in telemetry (`telemetry-git-version`) · +63/−1

Adds a best-effort `git_version` property to telemetry events: `gitVersion(ctx)` runs `git --version` with a 5s timeout and returns `""` on any failure; `parseGitVersion` extracts the version token; `SendEvent` attaches it only when non-empty. Privacy docs updated; parsing well-tested.

**What I verified:**
- **Correctness.** `parseGitVersion` validates shape (`len>=3`, `fields[0]=="git"`, `fields[1]=="version"`) and returns `fields[2]` — correct for all documented formats including the Windows variant (`2.45.1.windows.1` kept whole) and Apple suffix (`2.39.3`, suffix dropped). Edge cases (empty, wrong prefix, missing token) all return `""`. Solid table-driven test.
- **Best-effort isolation.** `gitVersion` bounds with `context.WithTimeout(5s)` and returns `""` on any error; `SendEvent` guards the nil `Properties` map before adding the key. A missing/hanging/garbled git never blocks telemetry — exactly as described.
- **No latency impact on the user.** `SendEvent` runs only inside the hidden `__send_analytics` **detached subprocess** (`root.go:166`, spawned via `spawnDetachedAnalytics`), so the new `git --version` subprocess and its 5s timeout live entirely in the background analytics process — it adds nothing to the user's actual command. The latency concern that would normally apply here is moot.
- **Privacy.** Git version is non-identifying; the privacy doc's "Captured per command" list is updated accurately, and the "Not captured" list (prompts, paths, source) is untouched.

**Trivial nits (not worth posting):**
- `gitVersion` (the exec+timeout wrapper) isn't directly tested — but it's a thin wrapper over `parseGitVersion` (which is) plus stdlib exec, so this is acceptable.
- No digit-shape validation on the version token (e.g. `git version foo` would record `foo`) — astronomically unlikely from real git and harmless for telemetry.

Nothing here rises to a medium. The change is conservative, correctly isolated to the detached sender, and well-tested. I haven't posted anything — and I don't think there's a finding worth posting, but say the word if you'd like either nit recorded on the trail.

## SUMMARY

This is well-structured, carefully-commented code that clearly had thought put into the security-sensitive bits (the `hostFromPublicURL` userinfo-injection guard, the `validateClusterHost` reuse, the env-token-aware auth resolution). The accessibility requirement is satisfied: every `huh` form in the wizard goes through `NewAccessibleForm` (→ `uiform.New`), and the wizard correctly fails fast via `interactive.CanPromptInteractively()` before touching auth or the network, with a clean pointer at the non-interactive form. The control-plane core-resolution concern is handled correctly — the displayed "Signed in as … via {coreURL}" comes from `resolveAuthStatusTarget`, which (per CLAUDE.md) applies ENTIRE_TOKEN-first precedence itself, and the actual API calls go through `coreapi.New()`, which resolves the same way, so the displayed core can't diverge from where requests go. Clone URLs are plain `entire://` placement URLs with no embedded credentials, so printing them is safe; no secrets are logged. Error handling is consistent (SilentError for already-printed/cancelled paths, `renderCoreError` for API errors). I found no critical or high-severity issues — the items below are medium and low. **MEDIUM — Region-picker default pre-selection is silently discarded when the catalog has no `is_default` for the caller's jurisdiction, and the cross-product can fan out very large with no confirmation.** `repo_mirror_create_wizard.go` ~line 250 (`runMirrorCreateWizard`) → `mirrorTargets`. Each `CreateMirror` is idempotent on (upstream, cluster) so this isn't catastrophic, but there's no "About to create N mirrors — proceed?" gate, and a mis-click in the multi-select is unrecoverable through the wizard. If `CreateMirror` succeeds but the subsequent clone wait times out or the clone reaches `failed`/`suspended`, `res.err` is set and the run exits non-zero via `NewSilentError(fmt.Errorf("%d mirror(s) failed"))` — but the placement *was* registered on the cluster and is left in place. There is no rollback and no message telling the user the placement exists despite the "failed" status. This is defensible (a timed-out clone may still complete server-side), but the results table shows `timed out`/`failed` with a clone URL present, which is ambiguous about whether the placement persists. - `multiSelectHeight` `headerSlack = 3` is a heuristic for title + wrapped description; on a very narrow terminal a long description could wrap to 3+ lines and still clamp. Edge case, low impact.
- Test coverage is solid on the pure helpers (`selectableAvailableRepos`, `hostFromPublicURL`, `clusterChoices`, `mirrorTargets`, `clustersToRegions`, non-TTY progress) and the TTY-refusal guard, with real assertions rather than construction-only. ## SUMMARY

This PR's in-scope delta is solid and, notably, **reduces** the security surface rather than expanding it. The headline probe refactor replaces a data-plane smart-HTTP `info/refs` poll — which minted short-lived repo-scoped pull tokens, carried them in redirect `Location` userinfo, and needed `checkProbeRedirect` to keep them inside the cluster trust domain — with a single authenticated control-plane `GetMirror` status poll per tick. That eliminates the token-in-URL/redirect-leak vector entirely and is gated by a new `Mirror.status` enum that the spec, generated code (schema/validator/decoder/JSON), and consuming code all agree on; the generated delta is a clean ogen regeneration with no hand-edits. The new `entire auth token` command reuses the existing `resolveAuthStatusTarget`, which already applies the env-token-first precedence and never re-resolves via the buggy `auth.ResolveControlPlaneTarget`, and it prints the bearer only to stdout (errors/hints to stderr, no `logging.*` calls) so secrets aren't logged. Tests are real (scripted fake `GetMirror`, exhaustive status coverage, correct not-parallel annotations on the two tests that mutate package/env state). I found **no medium-or-higher issues** — only minor nits. Overall judgment: **APPROVE.**

## MEDIUM+ FINDINGS

None.

I specifically checked the highest-risk items and they are clean:
- **No token logging/printing leak.** `auth token` writes only `target.token` to `cmd.OutOrStdout()`; the not-logged-in hint and all errors go to `cmd.ErrOrStderr()`. No `logging.*` call touches the token. It enforces `RequireSecureURL` before emitting a bearer for a non-`--insecure` core, mirroring `auth status`.
- **No credential-bearing mirror URL echoed.** The refactor removed the only place a pull token entered a URL (the data-plane probe + its redirect chain).
- **Core resolution is correct for display.** Resolution flows through `resolveAuthStatusTarget` (env-token-first), not `auth.ResolveControlPlaneTarget`.
- **Probe behavior preserved/improved.** First poll is immediate; `processing` keeps waiting; `ready`/`failed`/`suspended` are terminal; transient `GetMirror` errors are tolerated up to `maxConsecutivePollErrors` then surfaced; ctx cancel → SilentError, deadline → timeout error. The empty/absent-status case correctly keeps polling to the deadline.
- **Spec coherence.** `Mirror.status` enum (`processing|ready|failed|suspended`) added to spec; generated `MirrorStatus` const set, `OptMirrorStatus`, `Validate()`, and `decodeGetMirrorResponse` all match; no generated file hand-edited.

## LOW NITS

- **`cmd/entire/cli/auth_token_test.go` ~52** — The "not logged in" subtest relies on the empty-`contexts.json` early return in `resolveStatusTarget` to avoid ever calling the keychain, rather than explicitly installing the file token backend (`tokenstore.UseFileBackendForTesting`) or `keyring.MockInit`. It's safe today (and the in-process `testdirs` net covers it), but a future change that makes the not-logged-in path consult the keychain before checking contexts would silently start touching the dev's real keychain. Consider adding the file-backend setup defensively, matching the pattern other auth tests use.
- **`cmd/entire/cli/auth.go` ~140 (doc comment)** — The `newAuthTokenCmd` doc says it "resolves the same bearer the API client would." That's true for the env-token and active-context cases, but the API client (`coreapi.NewForCluster`) can also target a specific cluster's core, which `auth token` does not model. Minor wording imprecision; not a behavior bug since the command has no cluster flag.
- **`cmd/entire/cli/repo_mirror_probe.go` ~86 (comment)** — "mirrorStatusGetter is the slice of *coreapi.Client" reads as a typo for "the slice **of methods** / the subset of `*coreapi.Client`." Trivial.

No CLAUDE.md inaccuracy: the `auth token` description (hidden; honors `ENTIRE_TOKEN` else refreshed active-context login JWT) matches the implementation.</result>

Both reviews are in. Here's the consolidated result for PR #1518 / trail 659.

## PR #1518 — "chore(coreapi): refresh OpenAPI spec and regenerate client" (+1686/−648 → main, CI green)

**Verdict: approve, 2 medium findings (both in the wizard).** Despite the "chore" title, this is a real feature PR — and a good one. Notably, the probe refactor **reduces** the security surface, and the auth/spec half is clean.

### Auth + probe + spec half — clean, no findings ✅
- **Probe refactor is a security improvement.** It replaces a data-plane `info/refs` poll (which minted short-lived repo-scoped pull tokens, carried them in redirect `Location` userinfo, and needed `checkProbeRedirect` to keep them in-domain) with a single authenticated control-plane `GetMirror` status poll. That **eliminates the token-in-URL / redirect-leak vector entirely.** Polling behavior is preserved (immediate first poll, `processing` keeps waiting, `ready`/`failed`/`suspended` terminal, transient errors tolerated to a cap, ctx-cancel/deadline handled).
- **New `entire auth token` command is safe.** Writes the bearer only to stdout, hints/errors to stderr, no `logging.*` touches the token, and enforces `RequireSecureURL`. Core resolution goes through `resolveAuthStatusTarget` (env-token-first) — not the buggy `ResolveControlPlaneTarget`.
- **Spec delta is coherent.** Adds a `Mirror.status` enum (`processing|ready|failed|suspended`); the generated schema/validator/decoder/JSON all match a clean ogen regen with no hand-edits, and the consuming code uses the `OptMirrorStatus` wrapper correctly.

### Mirror-create wizard half — 2 medium findings
The wizard itself is well-built: every form uses `NewAccessibleForm`, it fails fast via `CanPromptInteractively()` before touching auth/network, clone URLs are plain `entire://` placements (no embedded creds), and core resolution is consistent. But:

**[medium] No confirmation before the repo×region create fan-out** — `repo_mirror_create_wizard.go` ~L250 (`mirrorTargets`)
The wizard builds the full cross-product of selected repos × selected regions and immediately fires `CreateMirror` for all of them (concurrency 8) with no summary/confirm step. Selecting 10 repos × 4 regions silently registers 40 placements; a multi-select mis-click is unrecoverable through the wizard. `CreateMirror` is idempotent on (upstream, cluster) so it's not catastrophic, but an "About to create N mirrors — proceed?" gate before the fan-out would prevent costly mistakes.

**[medium] Partial-failure leaves registered placements with ambiguous messaging** — `repo_mirror_create_wizard.go` ~L370-470 (`createOneMirror`/`reportMirrorResults`)
If `CreateMirror` succeeds but the clone wait times out or reaches `failed`/`suspended`, the run exits non-zero ("N mirror(s) failed") — but the placement *was* registered on the cluster and is left in place with no rollback and no message saying so. The results table shows `timed out`/`failed` alongside a clone URL, which is ambiguous about whether the placement persists. A one-line note that registered-but-not-ready placements remain and the create is idempotent (safe to retry) would resolve it.

### Low nits
- No direct test of `createOneMirror`'s status→result branching (ready/empty/registered/suspended/failed/timed-out) — the most logic-dense part, currently only covered indirectly; a table test against the injectable `awaitMirrorReady` seam would lock it in.
- `auth_token_test.go` "not logged in" subtest relies on the empty-`contexts.json` early return rather than explicitly installing the file token backend — safe today, but a defensive `tokenstore.UseFileBackendForTesting` would guard against a future change consulting the keychain first.
- Minor doc/comment imprecisions in `auth.go` (~L140) and `repo_mirror_probe.go` (~L86).

### Process note
Worth flagging on the PR itself: the **"chore: regenerate" title undersells ~900 lines of hand-written feature work** (the wizard + auth command). That label invites a rubber-stamp review — retitling to something like "feat(mirror): interactive mirror-create wizard + auth token command" would set correct reviewer expectations.

Good push — I checked, and you're right to make me verify, but the conclusion holds: **these files are hand-written, not generated.**

Evidence:
- None of the nine changed `cmd/entire/cli/` files carry the `// Code generated … DO NOT EDIT` marker (grep count = 0 for each). Every one starts directly with `package cli` followed by hand-style imports.
- Generated ogen output in this repo lives **only** under `internal/coreapi/` as `oas_*_gen.go` (plus the `spec/*.json`) — and those are exactly the files that *do* carry the marker. The `cmd/entire/cli/` package is the hand-authored CLI; there's no codegen that emits into it.
- The content itself is bespoke logic, not codegen output: `repo_mirror_create_wizard.go` builds multi-step `huh` forms with `NewAccessibleForm`, custom validation, a concurrency-bounded create fan-out, and a progress/spinner UI; `auth.go` adds the `entire auth token` cobra command; `repo_mirror_probe.go` is a refactor of the poll loop. ogen does not produce any of that.

So the split stands: ~90% hand-written feature code (wizard + auth command + probe refactor), and the small `internal/coreapi/oas_*_gen.go` + spec delta is the only generated part. That's also what makes the "chore: regenerate client" title misleading — the substantive, reviewable code here is human-authored.

The two medium findings from the wizard review (no confirm before the N-mirror fan-out; ambiguous partial-failure messaging) therefore stand as real review items. Want me to post them to trail 659?

3	This repo contains the CLI for Entire.
4	
5	## Architecture
6	
7	- CLI built with github.com/spf13/cobra and github.com/charmbracelet/huh
8	
9	## Key Directories
10	
11	### Commands (`cmd/`)
12	
13	- `entire/`: Main CLI entry point. Also home to kubectl-style external-command resolution (`entire <name>` → `entire-<name>` on PATH) — see [External Commands](docs/architecture/external-commands.md).
14	- `entire/cli`: CLI utilities and helpers (Cobra commands, helpers, group roots)

16	- `entire/cli/agent`: agent implementations (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Factory AI Droid, Copilot CLI, Pi) - see [Agent Integration Checklist](docs/architecture/agent-integration-checklist.md) and [Agent Implementation Guide](docs/architecture/agent-guide.md)

18	- `entire/cli/checkpoint`: checkpoint storage abstractions (ephemeral and persistent)
19	- `entire/cli/session`: session state management
20	- `entire/cli/integration_test`: integration tests (simulated hooks)
21	- `e2e/`: E2E tests with real agent calls (see [e2e/README.md](e2e/README.md))
22	
23	### Command Layout
24	
25	The visible CLI is organized around five noun groups plus a small set of
26	top-level verbs. The groups are the canonical home for each verb; legacy
27	top-level shortcuts remain functional but hidden, and emit a deprecation hint
28	pointing at the canonical group form. Newer experimental command families are
29	discoverable through `entire labs` and may remain hidden from root help while
30	their canonical paths are still runnable.
31	
32	- `session` (alias: `sessions`): `list`, `info`, `tokens`, `stop`, `attach`, `resume`, `current`.
33	  `resume` with a branch arg switches to it and resumes its session; with no arg
34	  it opens an interactive picker of stopped sessions (across all worktrees),
35	  resolving each to its branch and pointing at the owning worktree when the
36	  branch is checked out elsewhere. Resume keeps an existing local session log
37	  as-is by default (`--force` overwrites it from the checkpoint).
38	- `checkpoint` (aliases: `cp`, `checkpoints`): `list`, `explain`, `tokens`, `search`, plus
39	  the deprecated `rewind` (functional, prints a cobra deprecation message, will
40	  be removed in a future release)
41	- `agent`: bare opens the interactive agent selector, plus `list`, `add`, `remove`
42	- `configure`: bare prints help and a hint pointing at `entire agent`; flags
43	  manage non-agent settings (telemetry, git-hook installation mode, strategy
44	  options, summary provider). Agent CRUD lives under `entire agent`.
45	- `auth`: `login`, `logout`, `status`, `contexts`, `use`. `logout` takes
46	  `--everywhere` (revoke every session on the active core, not just the
47	  current one) and `--all-contexts` (log out of every saved login)
48	- `doctor`: bare runs the scan-and-fix flow, plus `trace`, `logs`, `bundle`
49	
50	Experimental command families advertised through `entire labs`:
51	
52	- `tokens`: `profile` (hidden from root help while token diagnostics mature)
53	
54	Top-level lifecycle and standalone commands: `enable`, `disable`, `status`,
55	`login`, `logout`, `clean`, `version`, `dispatch`, `activity`, `help`,
56	`configure`.
57	
58	Hidden top-level shortcuts (functional, emit a one-line deprecation hint):
59	`resume` → `session resume`, `attach` → `session attach`, `explain` →
60	`checkpoint explain`, `trace` → `doctor trace`.
61	Cobra-native aliases (no hint): `sessions` → `session`, `cp`/`checkpoints` →
62	`checkpoint`. The `search` top-level remains hidden without a hint.
63	
64	Deprecated top-level commands (functional, print a cobra deprecation message):
65	`reset` → `clean`, and `rewind` (no replacement, announces removal — same
66	deprecation as `checkpoint rewind`).
67	
68	Hidden infrastructure commands: `hooks`, `trail`,

70	
71	The `hideAsAlias(cmd, canonical)` helper in `cmd/entire/cli/aliascmd.go`
72	marks a command Hidden and sets cobra's `Deprecated` field so the hint
73	renders to stderr on every invocation while the command stays functional.
74	Diagnostic subcommands live alongside `doctor.go` as `doctor_logs.go` and
75	`doctor_bundle.go`. Group roots and noun-group children live in files

77	
78	## Tech Stack
79	
80	- Language: Go 1.26.x
81	- Build tool: mise, go modules
82	- Linting: golangci-lint
83	
84	## Development
85	
86	### Running Tests
87	
88	```bash
89	mise run test
90	```
91	
92	### Running Integration Tests
93	
94	```bash
95	mise run test:integration
96	```
97	
98	### Running All Tests (CI)
99	
100	```bash
101	mise run test:ci
102	```
103	
104	This runs unit tests, integration tests, and the E2E canary (Vogon agent) in sequence. Integration tests use the `//go:build integration` build tag and are located in `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/`.
105	
106	### Running E2E Canary Tests (Vogon Agent)
107	
108	The Vogon agent is a deterministic fake agent that exercises the full E2E test suite without making any API calls.
109	
110	```bash
111	mise run test:e2e:canary           # Run all E2E tests with the Vogon agent
112	mise run test:e2e:canary TestFoo   # Run a specific test
113	```
114

116	- **No API calls, no cost** — safe to run freely, unlike real agent E2E tests
117	- **If a canary test fails, the bug is in the CLI or test infrastructure**, not in an agent
118	- Located in `e2e/vogon/` (binary) and `cmd/entire/cli/agent/vogon/` (Agent interface)
119	- The binary parses prompts via regex, creates/modifies/deletes files, and fires lifecycle hooks

121	
122	### Running E2E Tests (Only When Explicitly Requested)
123	
124	**IMPORTANT: Do NOT run E2E tests proactively.** E2E tests make real API calls to agents, which consume tokens and cost money. Only run them when the user explicitly asks for E2E testing.
125	
126	```bash

Here's what PR #1507 ("Add checkpoint format compatibility checks", merged 2026‑06‑24) changed about how `resume` behaves.

## The core idea
It adds a new `checkpointpolicy` package that gates **every checkpoint read** on a format-version check. Checkpoint versions are strings like `<family>-v<major>` (e.g. `branch-v1`). The only currently read-supported format is `branch-v1`:
```go
var readFormats = map[CheckpointFormat]bool{ branchV1Format: true }  // branch-v1 only
```
`EnsureCanReadVersion(checkpointID, version)`:
- treats an **empty** version as `branch-v1` (so old checkpoints with no version field still read — no regression),
- returns a typed `unsupportedVersionError` if the version is unparseable or not in the read set, with the message *"checkpoint X uses unsupported checkpoint_version "branch-v2": not read-supported by this Entire CLI"*.

This is **forward-compatibility protection**: when a future CLI starts writing `branch-v2` (or `refs-v*`) checkpoints, today's CLI will refuse to resume them with a clear message instead of silently misreading the data.

## How that changes `resume` specifically

**1. The version gate is now applied on the resume read path.** `readCheckpointInfoFromStore` (the function resume uses to load checkpoint metadata) now calls `EnsureCanReadVersion(...)` right after reading the summary. So an unsupported checkpoint can't proceed into a resume.

**2. An unsupported version is now a hard, clearly-surfaced error — not a silent fallthrough.** Previously, any metadata-read failure was logged at debug and fell through to the generic "metadata not available / check remote" paths, so a too-new checkpoint would look like a confusing "nothing to resume." Now resume specifically detects `checkpointpolicy.IsUnsupportedVersion(err)` and returns it immediately:
- `resumeByCheckpointID` — returns the error instead of pointlessly trying the remote.
- `resumeFromCurrentBranch` — same on the store read.
- `checkRemoteMetadata` — tracks an `unsupportedVersionErr` across all its fetch/read attempts and, after exhausting options, returns *that* instead of the generic "git fetch entire/checkpoints/v1" hint. So even a checkpoint that only exists on the remote gives the user a clear "upgrade your CLI" message.
- `resumeSingleSession` — now reads the checkpoint summary and runs the version gate **before** reading the raw session log.

Net effect: `entire resume` / `session resume` against a checkpoint from a newer CLI fails loudly and understandably ("unsupported checkpoint_version, this CLI can't read it") instead of behaving as if there's nothing to resume.

**3. Stricter handling of the squash-merge multi-checkpoint case.** `resolveLatestCheckpoint` (used when a commit carries several checkpoint IDs) was changed from "skip any checkpoint whose metadata fails to read, resume from the latest of the rest" to fail-fast. Its signature went from `(*CheckpointInfo, error)` to `(*CheckpointInfo, bool, error)`:
- on a read error for **any** candidate (including unsupported version) → it now returns the error and resume aborts, rather than silently `continue`-ing past it;
- `found == false` (no error, simply no metadata resolvable) → still falls back to the "metadata not available" + remote-check path as before.

So in a squash-merge commit, if one of the checkpoints in the set is unreadable/too-new, resume no longer silently resumes a *different* (possibly older) checkpoint — it surfaces the problem.

**4. Cosmetic:** the multi-checkpoint message was reworded to "resuming from the latest checkpoint (N older checkpoint(s) skipped)".

## Worth knowing
The same version gate was added to `explain`, `rewind`, and `manual_commit_rewind.go` in this PR (so they reject too-new checkpoints consistently), but the resume-path changes above are the ones that affect the resume command. The unsupported-version error is returned as a normal error (not a `SilentError`), so `main.go` prints it to the user.

One subtle behavior change to keep in mind: resume is now **stricter** in the squash-merge case — a single unreadable checkpoint in a multi-checkpoint commit aborts the whole resume rather than degrading to "resume what I can." That's intentional (avoids resuming the wrong session), but it's a real behavioral difference from before the PR.

content.text:
Good question — the key is *where the version actually lives*. Here's that path explained properly.

## The version is data inside the checkpoint metadata, stored locally

The `checkpoint_version` isn't something you query the server for — it's a field written into the checkpoint's own metadata (`metadata.json`) when the checkpoint is created. That metadata is committed to the **`entire/checkpoints/v1` branch, which is a local git ref**. So reading the version is just reading a local git blob; no network is involved as long as that metadata is present locally (the common case — your own checkpoints, or any already-fetched ones).

That's why the gate can run before the remote: the version is already in hand the moment you read the checkpoint locally.

## The actual call chain (local-first)

In `resumeByCheckpointID`:

1. **Open the local store.** `checkpoint.Open(...)` → `stores.Persistent` is the local `entire/checkpoints/v1` ref. `promoteRemoteTrackingPrimary` may advance the local primary ref to match an already-fetched remote-tracking ref — still a **local** ref operation, no fetch.
2. **Read locally + gate.** `readCheckpointInfoFromStore(ctx, store, checkpointID)` calls `checkpoint.ReadCheckpoint(ctx, store, checkpointID)`, which returns a `CheckpointSummary` whose `CheckpointVersion` came straight out of the local metadata blob. Then immediately:
   ```go
   if err := checkpointpolicy.EnsureCanReadVersion(checkpointID.String(), summary.CheckpointVersion); err != nil {
       return nil, err   // unsupported-version error
   }
   ```
3. **Branch on the failure type.** Back in `resumeByCheckpointID`:
   ```go
   metadata, err := readCheckpointInfoFromStore(ctx, store, checkpointID)
   if err != nil {
       if checkpointpolicy.IsUnsupportedVersion(err) {
           return err            // ← version was readable locally and is too new: STOP, never touch remote
       }
       return checkRemoteMetadata(...)   // ← some *other* read failure (e.g. metadata not present locally): fall back to remote
   }
   ```

So the decision hinges on **why** the local read failed:
- **Unsupported version** → the version *was* read from local metadata, the gate rejected it → return immediately, remote never consulted.
- **Any other failure** (typically: the metadata simply isn't local yet) → fall through to `checkRemoteMetadata`.

## Why the remote path *also* has the version check

You can only know a checkpoint's version once you have its metadata. If the metadata isn't local at all, there's nothing to read the version from — you have to fetch it first. That's exactly what `checkRemoteMetadata` does: it fetches from origin, then runs the **same** `EnsureCanReadVersion` gate on the freshly-fetched metadata (which is why point 2 mentioned it tracks an `unsupportedVersionErr` across its fetch attempts).

So the rule is simply:

| Where the checkpoint metadata is | When the version is checked |
|---|---|
| Present locally (your checkpoints, or already fetched) | **Before** any remote call — local read + gate |
| Only on the remote | After fetching it (no other way to learn the version) |

In short: we can figure out the version before talking to the remote whenever the metadata is local, because the version is embedded in that metadata. The remote is consulted only when the metadata isn't local — and even then, the same gate runs on the fetched copy.

content.text:
## Review: trail 669 — Add `entire clone` / `entire repo clone` (`shimmying-gliding-mitten`) · ~520 hand-written lines

**Verdict: approve.** The security-sensitive parts — which is what this command is really about — are handled well. I had the review trace the credential/host flow end-to-end and it's sound:

- **No credential is embedded in the synthesized URL.** The clone URL is `entire://<host>/gh/<owner>/<repo>` with no token; the token exchange happens later inside `git-remote-entire`, which only sends credentials to a host whose `/.well-known` advertises a core **trusted by an existing local context** — and fails closed otherwise. So even a malicious/typo'd host can't receive a credential.
- **`--cluster` and the server-provided `ClusterHost` are both validated before any URL is built**, via `validateClusterHost`, which specifically defeats the `cluster@evil.com` userinfo-demotion trick (round-trip-to-bare-host check + DNS-label/IP validation).
- **`git clone` runs via exec argv (no `sh -c`)**, owner/repo/host are charset-restricted at the boundary (rejecting `?`, `#`, `..`, control chars), no token is logged, the multi-cluster picker uses `NewAccessibleForm` + `CanPromptInteractively()` (fails fast with a `--cluster` hint when non-interactive), and cross-cluster routing correctly uses `coreapi.NewForCluster`.

### Medium finding
**[medium] Missing `--` separator before positional args in the `git clone` invocation** — `repo_clone.go` ~`runGitClone` (~L270)
```go
args := []string{"clone", cloneURL}
if targetDir != "" { args = append(args, targetDir) }
```
There's no `--` before the positionals, so an argument starting with `-` could be parsed by `git clone` as a flag (argument injection). `cloneURL` is safe (always `entire://`…), but **`targetDir` is entirely user-controlled and unvalidated** — a value like `--upload-pack=…` would reach git as an option. Practical exploitability is low (cobra captures the known flags first), but the standard, cheap fix is `args := []string{"clone", "--", cloneURL}` with `targetDir` after — and it matches the careful security posture of the rest of this change. This is the one item I'd want addressed.

### Low/medium
**[low-medium] Unrelated lint change rides along** — `agentimport/agentimport.go` (−2), `.golangci.yaml` (+1): moving an `ireturn` suppression to a global `ifacecut` exclusion. Functionally net-neutral but unrelated to `entire clone` — looks like a rebase artifact/scope creep; better split out so blame/changelog attributes it correctly. Not blocking.

### Low nits
- The full-`entire://` passthrough path doesn't call `validateClusterHost` — **safe** (host safety is enforced downstream in `git-remote-entire`), but a one-line comment would save the next reader the trace.
- `validateClusterHost` doesn't validate the port component — cosmetic (a bad port only breaks the user's own clone; not a leak vector).
- No `RunE`-level test that the full-`entire://`-passthrough ignores `--cluster` and forwards the URL verbatim (the predicate is tested, not the contract).
- Genuine praise: the boundary hardening (the `cluster@evil.com` test case, case-folding normalization with a real cache-hit assertion, the `handleFormCancellation` guard against an empty-host `entire:///gh/...` clone, SilentError discipline) is well done, with comments explaining the threat model.

---
